App. P. 39(a) define it **differently within the same state** (Juneteenth), and one calendar per jurisdiction cannot serve both. **(5) ARIZONA** (added 2026-08-25) — Ariz. R. Civ. P. 6(a) says "legal holiday" and, on the text read, names no statute; the candidate A.R.S. 1-301 was not read. Same shape as Texas. **TWO JURISDICTIONS HAVE NOW ANSWERED IT THEMSELVES AND THEY ANSWER IT DIFFERENTLY, which is the strongest argument for asking this once rather than per state: WASHINGTON's CR 6(a) says outright "Legal holidays are prescribed in RCW 1.16.050" — an express cross-reference — and that statute then excludes its own decoys in subsection (7) ("may not be considered legal holidays for any purpose"); NORTH CAROLINA's Rule 6(a) instead asks whether "the courthouse is closed for transactions", so its statute is the wrong source entirely.** So the answer is not uniform and the question is really: which source does THIS rule's own words point at, and what do you do when they point at nothing? The common question: **when a court rule says "legal holiday" and points at nothing, does the general holiday statute supply the list, even where that statute is broader or narrower than what the courts actually observe?** Add the two Texas secondary-source rows to the same set while a lawyer is engaged **CATEGORY ADDED 2026-08-26, on Michael’s direction, covering MARYLAND and WISCONSIN together rather than as two new categories — they are the SAME SHAPE: a plausible-looking source that fails in the DANGEROUS direction.** Every jurisdiction above asks *which* list supplies “legal holiday”. These two ask something sharper: **the obvious source is not merely uncertain, it is affirmatively WRONG, and using it rolls deadlines LATE.** **(6) MARYLAND** — the intuitive path (Gen. Provisions § 1-302 + § 1-111) is wrong in BOTH directions at once: § 1-302 rolls only off Sunday, with no Saturday roll (→ EARLY), while § 1-111 adds Good Friday, Lincoln’s Birthday, Maryland Day and Defenders’ Day, four days that are NOT court holidays (→ LATE). Rule 1-203’s own committee note settles it — it **supersedes § 1-302**. Correct chain: Rule 1-203 → Rule 1-202(l) → **State Personnel & Pensions § 9-201**. **(7) WISCONSIN** — the wrongness is not which statute but **which TEST**. § 801.15(1)(b) rolls the last day unless it is “a day the clerk of courts office is closed” (a CLOSURE test), while the composed holiday definition in (1)(a) governs ONLY the sub-11-day intermediate-day exclusion. So the obvious move — drive the rollover off the holiday list — is the wrong basis, and because Wisconsin’s clerks of circuit court are COUNTY officers, any clerk open on a listed day means the rollover fires when the statute would not: **LATE**. The 1985 Law Revision Committee Note makes it worse rather than better, saying the amendment “will **permit** clerks to close their offices at these times” — permit, not require. **WHY THESE TWO BELONG WITH THE OTHERS AND NOT IN A ROW OF THEIR OWN:** the answer a lawyer gives to “when a rule says legal holiday and points at nothing, does the general statute supply the list?” is the same reasoning that answers “and what if the general statute is affirmatively the wrong one?” Splitting them would invite two inconsistent answers. **Both states are GATED-PASSED but deliberately UNSEEDED pending this** — see their own rows. Contrast the two that resolved safely: **MISSOURI**, where RSMo 9.010 is titled “Public holidays” (the identical lexical gap that helped kill Kentucky) but converges day-for-day with the state’s own schedule, so both readings agree; and **MASSACHUSETTS**, whose Rule 6(a) names its statute expressly. The distinction the lawyer needs to draw is CONVERGES vs DIVERGES, not NAMED vs UNNAMED. | L |

Every one of these produces plausible dates; only Louisiana’s is wrong, and only because a proviso buried mid-sentence scopes Saturday to some parishes. P. 1.1801 is one sentence pointing at **Iowa Code § 4.1(34)** (`first day` 0 hits, `legal holiday` 0 hits, `Sunday` 0 hits across 130 pages). § 4.1(34) sentence one rolls **ONLY SUNDAY**; sentence two rolls **Saturday + Sunday + clerk-closure + 11 named holidays** but is scoped to “**the commencement of an action … the FILING of a pleading or motion … or the perfecting or filing of an appeal**”. **Iowa’s answer and discovery deadlines are SERVICE deadlines** — R. 1.303(1) “shall **serve** … within 20 days”, and R. 1.509 says outright “**Answers shall not be filed**; however, they shall be **served**”. So the *n*th deadline depends on the *(n−1)*th ACTUAL FILING DATE, indefinitely. **Every seeded jurisdiction computes ONE date from ONE caller-supplied trigger.** Maryland’s chained discovery floor was logged as the highest-stakes shape found in any gate because ONE LIMB depended on another rule’s output; **Connecticut’s entire pleading cadence is that shape as the PRIMARY mechanism**. Seedable only as “30 days from the preceding pleading”, with a trigger named so nobody mistakes it for “30 days from the return day”, and a readme saying plainly that **Connecticut has no single answer deadline to compute**. Two domain-scoped variants ride the same sentence: **summary process 3 days, mortgage foreclosure 15 days**. And the **RETURN DAY is a Connecticut-specific concept fixed by Gen. Stat. § 52-48 (NOT read)** — it is a date stated in the writ, **not derivable from a service date**, so it must be caller-supplied and a seed must not silently equate the two. **BLOCKER TWO: THE ROLLOVER HAS NO HOLIDAY BASIS AT ALL.** Running the new standing weekend-coverage check, Connecticut fails the question’s premise: **“holiday” appears FIVE times in 699 pages and none of the five is definitional** (two are professional-conduct commentary on gifts, one is juvenile detention). Sec. 63-2 and Sec. 7-17 both roll on **“a day when the office of the clerk … is closed”**. Weekends therefore come out right by accident of fact (offices are shut), but **encoding Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-4’s list for the rollover would risk rolling LATE if a clerk’s office is in fact open on a listed day — the Wisconsin hazard**. Sec. 7-17 says offices close “during weeks which include a legal holiday” but **never says which days**. Correct basis is the **Judicial Branch’s published court-closure schedule**, making Connecticut ingest-not-derive alongside NC, NJ, MD and OK; plus a discretionary limb (closure authorized by the administrative judge “due to the existence of special circumstances”) that is unknowable → EARLY. **NO INTERMEDIATE-DAY EXCLUSION, STATED AFFIRMATIVELY:** Sec. 63-2 — “**Time shall be counted by calendar, not working, days.**” So the field is ABSENT, and unlike Minnesota (where it had to be inferred from a days-are-days rule) Connecticut says it outright. **NO SERVICE EXTENSION FOUND ANYWHERE IN THE PRACTICE BOOK** — zero hits for “days shall be added”, “shall be added to the prescribed” and “additional time after service”. Row note, not a mechanism. **ALSO NOT READ:** Gen. Stat. § 1-4; the discovery periods (Secs. 13-6, 13-9, 13-22/13-23, located but not read); and the Judicial Branch closure schedule itself. **UPDATE 2026-08-27 — PARTIALLY SEEDED, DELIBERATELY UNPROVISIONED (Hank).** The chain row is now live in `sql/sairnlaw_deadline_seed_connecticut.json` — ONE row, `ct-pb-10-8-advance-from-preceding-pleading`, trigger `filing_of_preceding_pleading` (named at length so it cannot be read as `return_day`), 30 calendar days forward, new standard `ct_pb_63_2` (`impl: frcp_6a`, **no** `short_period_exclusion_days`), `effective_from` **2014-01-01** from Sec. 10-8’s own amendment line. **NO `ct` CALENDAR WAS CREATED AND THAT IS THE HOLD:** `rollOff()` consults the calendar BEFORE it looks at the weekday, so Connecticut refuses `NOT_PROVISIONED` on **every** date, not just weekends — the Wisconsin hazard cannot be walked into. `api/_lib/deadline-connecticut.test.js` (26 assertions) asserts that on a **Tuesday** landing as well as a weekend one and **FAILS IF ANYONE LOADS A `ct` CALENDAR**. Oklahoma (~4.1M), statutory civil procedure (Oklahoma Pleading Code, Title 12). **OSCN — the Oklahoma State Courts Network — publishes Titles 12 and 25 free on plain curl** with per-section Historical Data, and its title indexes list every section with its CiteID, so navigation is mechanical rather than guesswork. **IT HAS LOUISIANA’S SHAPE:** 12 O.S. § 2006(A)(1) rolls the last day only if it is “a legal holiday as defined by Section 82.1 of Title 25 … or any other day when the office of the court clerk does not remain open” — **Saturday and Sunday are NOT named**, exactly the structure that blocked Louisiana one gate earlier. **ONE CLAUSE SAVES IT:** 25 O.S. § 82.1(A) opens “The designation and dates of holidays in Oklahoma shall be as follows: **Each Saturday, Sunday**, …” — both weekend days, statewide, no county qualification. So the rollover reaches them and **the engine’s `isWeekend()` is correct here**, by a different textual route than any common-law state. **RECORD THIS AS A PATTERN, NOT A ONE-OFF:** three states running have had the weekend INSIDE the holiday list rather than beside it — Louisiana (Sunday only, parish-scoped Saturday → **blocked**), Oregon (Sunday in the list but Saturday also named separately in the rule → safe), Oklahoma (both, statewide → safe). **The gate question is no longer “does the rule name Saturday and Sunday” but “if it doesn’t, does the holiday statute cover both, everywhere?”** **EXCLUSION IS ELEVEN DAYS** (with TN/AZ/WI/AL), **and SIX SECTIONS ARE EXPRESSLY CARVED OUT of it** — §§ 765, 990.3, 1148.4, 1148.5, 1148.5A and 1756 count every intermediate day regardless of length. An *enumerated* opt-out, narrower than Louisiana’s open-ended “expressly excluded” and Minnesota’s open-ended opt-in, but still something a standard-level flag cannot express. None is in a first civil batch so it is recordable rather than blocking — **but seeding one later without noticing would apply an exclusion the statute removes, computing LATE**. The clerk-closure limb sits in BOTH the rollover and the exclusion and is a **partial-closure** test (“does not remain open … until the regularly scheduled closing time”), same breadth as Oregon’s; additional to the list rather than a replacement, so EARLY. **THE CALENDAR IS NOT FULLY DERIVABLE, FOR TWO INDEPENDENT REASONS.** (a) **The Christmas rule is the most complex encountered anywhere** — Dec 25, plus “the day before **or** after Christmas if Christmas is not on a Saturday or Sunday”, plus “the Thursday and Friday before Christmas if Christmas is on a Saturday”, plus “the Monday and Tuesday after Christmas, if Christmas is on a Sunday” — two or three holidays depending on the weekday, and **the general both-ways shift expressly does NOT apply to Christmas**. The before-or-after choice is simply not in the statute. (b) **§ 82.1(B) requires the Governor to issue an Executive Order EACH YEAR** specifying the dates — the **New Jersey annual-order shape layered on a statute** — and it is the only thing that resolves the Christmas choice. So Oklahoma is **ingest-per-year**, joining NJ, NC and MD, and is the first to be so for a **single day inside an otherwise derivable list**. The presidential limb (“the Governor **may** issue an Executive Order”) is discretionary and ad hoc on top: EARLY. **DO NOT ENCODE JUNETEENTH ON 19 JUNE.** Oklahoma’s is 25 O.S. **§ 82.4**, “**the third Saturday in June**”, a separate section — and § 2006 defines legal holiday by reference to **§ 82.1 only**. Practically it changes nothing because the third Saturday is already a holiday under “Each Saturday”, so it is **functionally invisible to deadline computation** — but encoding a 19 June holiday by analogy to the ten other seeded states would add a non-holiday and compute **LATE**. Also **no Columbus/Indigenous Peoples Day at all** (as in Oregon), and **the day after Thanksgiving IS statutory** (as in SC, unlike MN where it is a branch option). **SERVICE: +3 for mail, THIRD-PARTY COMMERCIAL CARRIER and electronic means** — ninth distinct answer on electronic service and the only one naming commercial carrier as its own category — period-lengthening, not Alabama’s federal after-expiry order. **BUT § 2006(D)’s proviso is a different TRIGGER, not a different amount:** where a summons and petition are served by mail, the answer runs from **the date of RECEIPT, or if refused the date of REFUSAL**, and takes **no +3**. Own row, or a caller supplying a service date computes EARLY. **AND THE ANSWER PERIOD CARRIES A PLAINTIFF’S ELECTION THE ENGINE CANNOT SEE:** § 2012(A) gives 20 days, but (A)(4) lets “the party requesting a summons to be issued … **elect** to have the answer served within **thirty-five (35) days** in lieu of the twenty” — a fact about what the requesting party chose, the same shape as Louisiana art. 1001’s 21-vs-30. **Two rows with unmissable names; guessing 35 where 20 applies computes LATE.** A defendant’s reservation of time adds a further 20 days while waiving defences — unseeable, but it only ever extends, so EARLY. **NOT DETERMINED:** the discovery periods (§§ 3233, 3234, 3236 — same source, effort remaining not a source problem); whether any of the six carved-out sections belongs in a civil batch; the current year’s Executive Order; and **25 O.S. § 82.2**, whose title suggests it bears on acts performable on holidays — § 2006 points only at § 82.1, but § 82.2 must be read to confirm it does not widen the definition **✅ SEEDED 2026-08-28 (Hank) — 9 rules, `sql/sairnlaw_deadline_seed_oklahoma.json`, new standards `ok_12_2006` and `ok_12_2006_d`, calendar 2026–2031 from `tools/gen_ok_calendar.py`. `deadline-oklahoma.test.js` 51/51.** All three gate conditions met. **(1) THE TWO FACTS THE ENGINE CANNOT DERIVE ARE FOUR SEPARATE ROWS, never one with a default** — the plaintiff’s 20-vs-35 election under § 2012(A)(4), and § 2006(D)’s proviso, which on MAILED process changes the **TRIGGER** to **receipt or refusal** rather than the amount. I then read the **2022 Supreme Court order “RE: Service by E-Mail in the Trial Courts”** (App. Case 2022-000029, 6 May 2022) end to end: paragraphs (a)–(f), and **no time-extension provision whatsoever**. Every seeded state keys on one list, or on two STATE lists (Wisconsin). This matters concretely — **Juneteenth and Columbus Day are federal holidays and are NOT in S.C. Code § 53-5-10**, so encoding only the state list would miss both and compute EARLY. **FIVE DAYS FOR MAIL, NOT THREE**, and the drafting Note says so: “the additional time … is increased from 3 to 5 days.” A three-day extension copied from a neighbour computes **two days EARLY on every mailed SC period**. It also reaches service on a **statutory agent**, which no other seeded rule does. **THE STATE LIST IS LONG AND DISTINCTIVE:** Confederate Memorial Day (10 May), the day after Thanksgiving **in the statute itself** (where Minnesota leaves it to a branch option), and a **THREE-DAY Christmas block, 24, 25 and 26 December** — no other seeded jurisdiction has any of these. **TWO CAVEATS ON THE SHIFT, both for the bundled holiday question rather than new categories:** § 53-5-30 shifts both ways but says “for all of the purposes aforesaid” in a section captioned about **presentment of bills, notes and checks**, so whether it reaches COURT deadlines is arguable on the text (a smaller cousin of the Maryland list-but-not-shift problem); and it shifts only “the holidays mentioned in Section 53-5-10”, i.e. the STATE half — the federal half has its own observance rules under 5 U.S.C. § 6103, so SC may need **two shift rules for two halves of one union**, which no seeded generator does. Reading across would compute LATE on 33/34 and EARLY on 36, where silence ADMITS. **THE THREE-DAY CHRISTMAS BLOCK (24, 25, 26 Dec — unique) COLLIDES under the shift in 2026, 2027 and 2028**; the generator deduplicates and records the merge. **In 2027 Christmas Day itself is not an emitted date** — 25 Dec is a Saturday so it merges back onto the 24th, and 26 Dec moves forward to Monday the 27th. Act 247 and through all Supreme Court Orders … in effect on August 5, 2026. Published and certified under s. 35.18.” Stronger than Missouri’s per-section version history or Maryland’s per-rule credits — nothing has to be cross-checked against a second source. **NO NEW ENGINE MECHANISM REQUIRED:** § 801.15(5) is VIRGINIA’s shape, not Missouri’s — mail +3 days, and fax/e-mail/e-filing **+1 day if the transmission is “completed between 5 p.m. and midnight”**, else +0. That is an AMOUNT that varies by clock, so it maps straight onto the existing `amount(method, ctx)` with `service_time`; the completion standard built for Missouri is NOT needed. **Fifth state, fifth answer on electronic service** (MA +3 in the time rule; TN service rule deems it mail → +3; MO +0 with a moved trigger; MD +0 and no cutoff; WI +1 on a clock). Found by the standing habit again, this time in reverse: § 801.14(2) — the service rule — has NO deeming and NO cutoff, because Wisconsin puts the cutoff in the TIME rule instead, the opposite of Missouri. **THE ONE THING TO SETTLE, AND IT IS THE DANGEROUS DIRECTION:** § 801.15(1)(b) uses TWO DIFFERENT TESTS in one subsection — the last day rolls unless it is **“a day the clerk of courts office is closed”** (a CLOSURE test, the North Carolina shape), while the carefully-composed holiday definition in (1)(a) governs ONLY the sub-11-day intermediate-day exclusion. **No seeded jurisdiction uses one basis for the rollover and another for the exclusion.** Wisconsin’s clerks of circuit court are COUNTY officers, so if any clerk is open on a listed day, encoding the list for rollover rolls **LATE**. (Closures not on the list run EARLY, which is safe.) The 1985 Law Revision Committee Note is exactly the wrong word for this purpose — the Good Friday/Dec 24/Dec 31 amendment “will **permit** clerks to close their offices at these times”, permit not require, which is why this cannot be waved through. **Three options, none chosen:** (1) treat the union list as a closure proxy and disclose the mismatch — needs checking that clerks actually close on every listed day; (2) seed only periods ≥ 11 days so the exclusion never fires, and disclose the rollover basis — reduces but does not remove the exposure; (3) refuse Wisconsin rollover entirely — safe, near-useless. **THE HOLIDAY DEFINITION IS A UNION OF THREE SOURCES** and neither list is a superset: § 801.15(1)(a) takes § 230.35(4)(a) OR § 995.20 “or both”, PLUS “a full day on Good Friday”. Only in 230.35(4)(a): **Dec 24 and Dec 31**. Only in 995.20: 3rd Mon Feb, **Juneteenth, Columbus Day, Veterans Day and TWO ELECTION DAYS**. And Good Friday is a FULL day only for time computation — 995.20 makes it just 11 a.m.–3 p.m. for worship, so encoding 995.20 alone would miss it. **Shift is SUNDAY-ONLY in both** (230.35(4)(a)(10) narrower still: only if Jan 1, Jul 4 or Dec 25 falls on Sunday) — **third state running** where carrying VA’s or WV’s both-ways shift would invent a Friday holiday and roll LATE. **County-scoped, same shape as MA’s Suffolk County:** 995.20 makes municipal election day a holiday “in every 1st class city” (Milwaukee) and lets counties of 750,000+ add holidays by ordinance — omitting runs EARLY, safe, same coverage treatment. **THE ANSWER RULE IS THE MOST BRANCH-HEAVY YET (§ 802.06(1)(a)):** 20 days default, 20 for a guardian ad litem from appointment, 20 for a cross-claim answer and for a reply, **45 for the state or a state officer/employee/agent**, and **45 “if a defendant in the action is an insurance company, or if any cause of action … is founded in TORT”**, plus 10 days after notice of the court’s action on a denied motion and 10 after service of a more definite statement. **The tort/insurer branch is the trap** — it turns on what the CLAIM IS ABOUT, not on service, which the engine cannot infer; getting it wrong reports 20 days when 45 is due (EARLY, so safe in direction but badly wrong for a user, and it is the branch a large share of civil filings actually fall in). Needs its own row with an unmissable trigger name, like Missouri’s three § 55.25(a) branches. **DISCOVERY IS ORDINARY:** §§ 804.08, 804.09 and 804.11 are all 30 days with a 45-day defendant floor, no outlier (unlike Missouri’s 45/45/60), silence ADMITS under 804.11, and every floor runs from **service of the summons and complaint — a caller-supplied date, NOT a computed one — so Wisconsin does NOT hit the Maryland chained-floor gap**. Short-period exclusion is **ELEVEN days**, matching TN and AZ, and Wisconsin explains why: a 1986 Judicial Council Note records the extension from 7 to 11 “to conform to that made in Rule 6 (a), F.R.C.P. in 1985” — **so the 7-vs-11 split across states is a VINTAGE ARTEFACT**, useful when gating the rest. **Not determined:** whether WI clerks of circuit court publish closure schedules per county or centrally (option 1 turns on it), and the § 801.18 e-filing subchapter was not read beyond 801.15(5)(b)’s reference. Secondary disclosables: the **“between 5 p.m. and midnight”** boundary at exactly 17:00 is genuinely ambiguous (Virginia’s “no later than”/“after” wording is not), and a transmission at 02:00 is NOT between 5 p.m. and midnight so adds nothing — a naive “after 5 p.m.” implementation gets that wrong | L |

Maryland’s second limb runs from “the date on which that party’s initial pleading or motion is **required**” — **the output of another rule** — and it is not a static offset: Rule 2-321 sets the answer at **30, 60 or 90 days** depending on how and where the defendant was served, and Rule 2-321(c) extends it further to “15 days after entry of the court’s order” on a Rule 2-322 motion or remand. So the floor is 45 / 75 / 105 days, or a date that depends on a ruling. **`resolve_periods` cannot express it** — its limbs take an event and a count, and neither limb can be “the result of computing rule X”. **Nothing seeded today handles a trigger that depends on another rule’s outcome.** **THE STAKES ARE WHY THIS IS ITS OWN ROW:** Rule 2-424 is self-executing — miss it and facts are **DEEMED ADMITTED** — so a floor guessed short computes **EARLY on the one rule where an early date silently forfeits the case on the merits**.
